title: Correction Reach: An Operational Framework for Downstream Corrigibility in LLM-Assisted Scholarly Communication
content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft, summarise, review, and transform scholarly text. At the same time, studies of retracted research show that problematic evidence can remain embedded in later reviews, guidelines, and other publications, while downstream correction is uncommon. Prior studies of downstream response in retraction cohorts generally use the citing publication as their unit and report different outcomes, such as correction, notification, or reply. We propose correction reach as an assertion-level construct: the extent to which a qualifying correction event prompts documented reassessment of downstream assertions that depend on the corrected source. The framework separates notification, reassessment, and effect. A descendant counts as reached when the dependency is examined and the decision is recorded, including a decision that no change is needed. A purposive critical review positions the construct against retraction propagation, citation distortion, provenance, and prior studies of downstream correction. We then specify a bounded denominator, observable reassessment events, correction latency, and three empirical designs. LLMs may increase the production and transformation of derivative claims, but they may also improve dependency mapping and updating. Their net effect on corrigibility is therefore an empirical question. Correction reach provides a common unit for studying downstream corrigibility.
